supportingExcerpt: Stress signals induce BH3-only proteins (BIM, PUMA, NOXA, BAD) that either inhibit anti-apoptotic BCL-2, BCL-XL, MCL-1 or directly activate BAX/BAK, which permeabilise the mitochondrial outer membrane, releasing cytochrome c to activate caspase-9 and executioner caspases.

Design (NEJM 2020): 1,174 patients with untreated stage II or III triple-negative breast cancer randomised 2 to 1 to pembrolizumab 200 mg or placebo every 3 weeks with four cycles of paclitaxel and carboplatin then four of doxorubicin or epirubicin with cyclophosphamide, surgery, then nine cycles of adjuvant pembrolizumab or placebo.

For breast resection, final margin status uses the oriented main specimen together with relevant separately submitted margins. Ink identifies cut surfaces. An old main-specimen edge may cease to be the final edge when an additional oriented strip is removed; if their relationship is unclear, preserve uncertainty and request surgical correlation.

In a fictional confirmed final edge with DCIS 0.7 mm from ink and no cancer at ink, the margin is narrow and negative rather than involved. Distance alone does not choose another operation. Conversely, invasive cancer at the confirmed outer edge of an additional lateral specimen remains a local margin finding even if a blood assay is negative.

Report invasive carcinoma and DCIS separately, including the named final edge, whether the component reaches ink and its distance in millimetres when measurable. At ink is involved; a small gap without cancer at ink is a narrow negative margin. Ink artefact, limited sampling, compression and unclear orientation can limit interpretation.

In FDA breast-trial guidance, ypT0/Tis ypN0 means no residual invasive cancer on haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) examination of the complete resected breast specimen and all sampled regional nodes after neoadjuvant systemic treatment. Residual DCIS is permitted. The stricter ypT0 ypN0 definition also excludes in situ cancer. Preserve the actual protocol and nodal assessment rules.

FDA's July 2020 revision 1 guidance concerns pCR endpoints for trial design and accelerated approval in high-risk early-stage breast cancer. It is not an individual treatment or cure rule. In the notation, y denotes assessment after neoadjuvant treatment and p denotes pathological assessment. Sections and stains consume finite tissue; incomplete sampling, unexamined nodes and mixed endpoint definitions can invalidate comparisons.

Residual DCIS can meet the invasive-clearance definition while still requiring separate margin assessment. In an otherwise qualifying specimen with DCIS but no breast invasion and no residual sampled-node cancer, the permissive definition is met and the stricter one is not. Neither pCR nor a negative local edge certifies cure or absence at every body site.

In fictional case A, no breast invasion, residual DCIS and no residual cancer in sampled nodes meet ypT0/Tis ypN0 but not ypT0 ypN0. In fictional case B, the same breast finding plus a 4-mm residual invasive nodal deposit meets neither combined endpoint. Identical DCIS-at-ink findings in either case remain a separate margin question.

Breast-only clearance is not the combined breast-and-node endpoint. Residual invasive cancer in a sampled node prevents that combined pCR result even when breast invasion is absent or a blood assay is negative. A small negative biopsy, imaging response and negative circulating tumour DNA are different observations.

Negative invasive margins and involved DCIS margins can coexist. A pCR definition permitting DCIS can coexist with a DCIS margin problem. The lymph-node capsule, a vessel lumen and a surgical cut edge are different boundaries. Margin status does not diagnose distant metastasis or whole-body clearance; completion excision, mastectomy and axillary surgery address different tissues.

RCB combines six post-treatment pathology inputs: two breast-bed dimensions in millimetres, overall cancer area percentage, in situ percentage of the cancer component, positive-node count and largest nodal metastasis diameter in millimetres. Distinguish continuous index from classes 0, I, II and III, and both from ypTNM stage or recurrence percentages.

For RCB, overall cancer cellularity estimates the area occupied by invasive plus in situ cancer within a defined residual breast bed. The in situ percentage instead uses the cancer component as denominator. Microscopic review can revise bed boundaries and should represent sparse as well as dense regions; selecting only a dense focus changes the measurement.

Invasive bed fraction equals overall cancer fraction multiplied by one minus the in situ fraction of cancer. In a fictional 100-unit bed with 20 units of cancer, 25% in situ means 5 bed units in situ and 15 invasive. The invasive share is 75% of cancer but only 15% of the whole bed. These idealised area units teach denominators, not counting instructions or the precision of a clinical estimate.

CAP states that RCB was not designed or validated for neoadjuvant endocrine treatment and advises against reporting its score or class there. Individual measurements such as cellularity may still describe residual disease. Use the official pathology assessment and calculator for unusual findings; low breast cellularity alone cannot establish nodal clearance or pCR.

Area occupied by cancer, the proportion of counted cells that are malignant and the fraction of sequenced DNA contributed by cancer have different denominators. A selected assay block may also differ from the whole residual bed. Do not enter an area-cellularity estimate as sequencing purity or describe 25% of cancer as 25% of the bed.

CAP 4.11 describes the RCB breast span as the two-dimensional extent of residual invasive carcinoma, excluding DCIS from the span. The MD Anderson microscopy protocol instead starts with the gross tumour bed, revises its boundaries microscopically and estimates invasive plus in situ cancer area in that bed, using the largest bed for multicentric disease. State the protocol and denominator rather than merging these wordings. The largest contiguous residual invasive focus without adjacent treatment fibrosis supplies ypT; the gross scar, that focus and an RCB bed are different measurements. For ypN, adjacent treatment fibrosis is likewise excluded from the contiguous staging dimension; RCB nodal measurement has its own rule.

CAP 4.11 describes the RCB breast span as the two-dimensional extent of residual invasive carcinoma, excluding DCIS from the span. The MD Anderson microscopy protocol instead starts with the gross tumour bed, revises its boundaries microscopically and estimates invasive plus in situ cancer area in that bed, using the largest bed for multicentric disease. State the protocol and denominator rather than merging these wordings. The largest contiguous residual invasive focus without adjacent treatment fibrosis supplies ypT; the gross scar, that focus and an RCB bed are different measurements.

Assessment connects pretreatment location, imaging or marker information, gross mapping, a sampling plan and microscopy. Sparse, scattered residual foci make arbitrary-section interpretation unreliable. A broad scar can contain residual invasive cancer without the whole scar being solid cancer.

After preoperative therapy, fibrosis, necrosis, inflammation and histiocytic aggregates can be response-related tissue changes. Residual viable carcinoma is a separate morphological assessment, not a culture test of every cell. Response changes and residual cancer can coexist; scarring alone does not establish that no cancer remains. Fibrosis means collagen-rich scarring, necrosis means dead tissue and histiocytes are tissue macrophages.

Breast and node response are reported separately. Nodal scarring or histiocytic aggregates without residual cancer can be consistent with prior treated involvement, but do not independently establish biopsy-proven baseline metastasis. Prior biopsy or other injury can also produce repair changes; a scar alone cannot establish a drug-specific effect.

The MD Anderson protocol estimates overall cellularity and in situ percentage to the nearest 10%, with additional 1% and 5% choices for low values. The 25% in situ example above is fictional denominator arithmetic outside those listed estimation increments. Its arithmetic remains 20 × 0.25 = 5 in situ and 20 - 5 = 15 invasive bed units. A separate protocol-aligned 20% in situ illustration would give 4 in situ and 16 invasive units. Neither should be confused with the RCB example using 50% in situ.

Retain the named bed, specimen, treatment setting, mapping and representative sections, overall area percentage and in situ share separately. Incomplete sampling, a misdefined bed and heterogeneous distribution can bias the estimate; staining or sampling consumes finite tissue. There is no universal low/high cellularity cutoff that alone selects treatment.

Cellularity alone supplies neither nodal burden, final margins, distant status, pCR nor an RCB score. CAP's residual-invasive RCB span excludes DCIS, while the MD Anderson protocol estimates invasive plus in situ area in a microscopically revised cancer bed. Neither is interchangeable with the largest contiguous ypT focus. CAP advises against RCB score/class after neoadjuvant endocrine therapy, although individual residual measurements may still be useful.

Lines of therapy describe successive treatment strategies under a clinical record or study's stated counting rule. First-line is the initial strategy for the specified disease setting. A later strategy may follow because treatment does not work, stops working or causes intolerable harm. The setting and reason for change belong beside the number.

In an advanced-cancer trial, first-line can mean no earlier systemic treatment for advanced disease, while previous treatment around surgery remains part of the exposure history and eligibility assessment. Several medicines, repeating cycles and planned blocks can belong to one strategy. A line count does not measure remaining life or establish that treatment options are exhausted.

A regimen specifies the treatment plan; a cycle is a defined interval of treatment and recovery. Neither a third infusion nor a third medicine automatically means third-line treatment. A planned switch between blocks differs from changing strategy after progression. Neoadjuvant and adjuvant describe roles around the main treatment, rather than first and second line.

In a fictional history, combination A precedes definitive surgery and medicine B follows it as part of one planned early-disease strategy. Years later, the first systemic strategy for metastatic disease is first-line metastatic under the stated rule of no earlier systemic metastatic treatment. A and B remain in the exposure history. The setting boundary changes what is being counted; it is not a universal rule for every switch or maintenance phase.

Keep four entries together: disease setting, strategy with start and stop dates, reason for change, and the counting convention. Maintenance, a pause, dose reduction or removal of one component must be interpreted under that convention. A database algorithm can draw boundaries differently from the clinical account, so preserve the actual events before assigning a number.

Before comparing studies labelled first-line or later-line, check prior exposure, eligibility, resistance history, tolerability and the comparator. Matching a drug name does not match the populations. To explain a line number, name the disease setting, earlier strategy and counting rule, rather than turning that history label into an individual forecast.

The assessment must match the branch. An imaging change needs its modality, baseline, acquisition time, units and protocol threshold; tissue response needs the sampled sites, adequacy and definition. A change in one lesion is not a complete patient-level assessment, and a blood assay measures circulating material. Predicted pathological complete response is not the surgical finding itself, and a negative biopsy describes only the tissue submitted. Strategy benefit needs a comparator, recurrence or survival endpoint, follow-up and harms. No universal response percentage supplies permission to omit treatment.

Consider a fictional early-surgery checkpoint requiring both a specified MRI criterion and an adequate negative biopsy. The scan meets its criterion, but the biopsy is inadequate. The combined AND rule is not met, because an uninterpretable input cannot be replaced by the favourable scan. This exercise supplies no numerical cutoff or treatment instruction; correct branch logic remains separate from evidence that acting on the rule improves clinical outcomes.

In the 2024 I-SPY2.2 phase 2 report, 106 participants received datopotamab deruxtecan with durvalumab in the first block for high-risk stage II or III breast cancer. Subtype-specific algorithms used serial magnetic resonance imaging volume change and core biopsy to redirect later blocks, including earlier surgery for participants predicted to have a high probability of complete pathological response. The endpoint was assessed at resection. This was a defined research strategy, not permission to cancel surgery or a demonstration of equivalent long-term survival.

Postoperative adaptation has different comparisons. CREATE-X selected residual HER2-negative invasive disease after chemotherapy; OlympiA selected high-risk germline BRCA1/2-associated HER2-negative disease; EA1131 did not demonstrate that platinum was noninferior or superior to capecitabine in its residual basal-subtype comparison. Those studies do not directly test adding their medicines to the complete pembrolizumab sequence. Risk, a plausible mechanism and eligibility do not independently establish added benefit.

KEYNOTE-522 tested a selected high-risk, previously untreated early-TNBC population, with chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab or placebo before surgery and pembrolizumab or placebo afterwards. Eight planned 3-week preoperative cycles and nine postoperative cycles correspond to about 24 and 27 weeks; delays and clinical decisions can alter actual timing. The U.S. label describes tumour-size and nodal eligibility and enrolment regardless of PD-L1 expression. A stage label alone is not a personal treatment instruction. The complete regimen comparison did not independently randomise its two phases.

The study question concerns the whole assigned sequence in previously untreated, non-metastatic stage II or III triple-negative breast cancer: T1c with N1 or N2, or T2 to T4 with N0 to N2, and performance status 0 or 1. The registry excludes prior checkpoint therapy and active autoimmune disease requiring systemic treatment in the preceding two years, among other criteria. There was one assignment of 784 people to pembrolizumab and 390 to placebo across preoperative chemotherapy, surgery and postoperative treatment, without a separate postoperative randomisation. Smaller node-negative tumours outside those entry criteria and metastatic disease are different settings. Entry did not require PD-L1 selection, and the high-risk early-stage indication in the prescribing information has no PD-L1 threshold.

Neoadjuvant treatment precedes the main treatment, usually surgery; adjuvant treatment follows the main treatment to reduce recurrence risk. Perioperative treatment spans the period around an operation. Neoadjuvant therapy can aim to reduce disease before an operation and provides response information from treated tissue. Adjuvant therapy aims to reduce risk from disease that may remain. A pathological response and a later clinical outcome are different endpoints.

Timing comparisons need the actual population, intervention and comparator. Liu’s two mouse breast-cancer models supported testing preoperative immunotherapy, not a universal human timing rule or proof that retained tumour antigen explains every clinical result. KEYNOTE-522 assigned a complete before-and-after pembrolizumab regimen against its comparator; that design does not independently randomize the two phases and cannot isolate each phase’s contribution.

Keep specimen collection, treatment administration and report issue as three dates. A biopsy collected before treatment remains a pretreatment sample even if its report arrives after surgery. Likewise, a planned treatment phase is not proof of administration: holds, substitutions and cancelled visits belong in the delivered record. Timing of a report cannot manufacture a post-treatment observation.

The BCL-2 family contains survival proteins, including BCL-2, BCL-XL and MCL-1; BH3-only stress mediators, including BIM, BID and PUMA; and pore-forming effectors BAX and BAK. In experimental cells, loss of both BAX and BAK blocked several mitochondrial apoptotic responses, rather than every possible form of death.

Cytochrome c moves from the mitochondrial intermembrane compartment, including crista stores, across the outer membrane to the cytosol. It does not begin in the matrix. The inner membrane separates these compartments; the spatial sketch is simplified, with no implied pore stoichiometry.

Intrinsic apoptosis involves mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilisation, cytochrome c release into the cytosol, apoptosome assembly and caspase-9 activation upstream of executioner caspases such as caspase-3 and caspase-7. Death-receptor signalling can activate caspase-8; BID cleavage links this route to mitochondria. Initiator and executioner roles differ.

A stain for BCL-XL measures abundance rather than survival dependence. BCL2 and BCL2L1 are different genes, and inhibitor selectivity matters. Souers and colleagues re-engineered dual BCL-2/BCL-XL inhibition into BCL-2-selective ABT-199, sparing human platelets; early tumour lysis in three refractory chronic lymphocytic leukaemia patients does not establish benefit in every tumour. A mitochondrial response, caspase marker, sustained killing and immune protection remain separate outcomes. Keep cell identity, timing, handling controls and later survival or regrowth with cleaved-caspase assays, membrane readouts and microscopy. Mitochondrial BH3 challenges test readiness under a defined protocol, rather than completed killing or clinical benefit.

Compare mechanism, morphology, immune consequence and living arrest separately. Apoptosis uses regulated dismantling; necrotic morphology describes boundary failure; ferroptosis requires iron-dependent lipid damage causing death; immunogenicity requires a compatible adaptive response; senescence is a living arrest. These categories are not mutually exclusive outcomes or a universal appearance-based classifier.

The 2020 consensus defines immunogenic cell death through the adaptive immune response, not merely the appearance of dead cells. Antigens, appropriately timed danger signals, antigen-presenting cells and a responsive host all matter. Apoptotic or other death machinery does not by itself classify the immune outcome.

Calreticulin exposure, ATP or HMGB1 release and interferon-related signals are useful mechanistic readouts, but none alone proves protective immunity. Functional cross-priming and appropriate in-vivo immune tests address later steps. The consensus distinguishes mouse vaccination models from established disease; neither a surrogate marker nor a positive mouse assay establishes clinical benefit in a person.

Surface calreticulin, released ATP and HMGB1 have distinct mechanistic roles in defined experiments. Calreticulin supported dying-cell uptake, ATP signalled through dendritic-cell P2X7/inflammasome pathways, and HMGB1/TLR4 supported processing and presentation. These are examples rather than a universal sufficient three-marker checklist. A DAMP is not automatically a tumour-specific antigen.

Death plus extracellular ATP does not establish a cancer vaccine. Danger signals, cross-priming, functional protection, distant control and patient benefit are separate claims. Even a positive mouse vaccination assay remains model-bound and does not select a clinical treatment.

In the consensus vaccination assay, remove residual inducing chemical and add no separate adjuvant before vaccinating immunocompetent syngeneic mice with dying tumour cells. Compare later challenge with living matched tumour cells in vaccinated and unvaccinated hosts, and test specificity with unrelated compatible tumour cells. Incidence and growth are functional readouts. Immune-competent versus deficient comparisons alone cannot isolate immunogenic death from other immunostimulation. Assays consume tumour-cell aliquots, supernatant or host-model material and report separate dead-cell fractions, signal concentrations or surface staining and challenge incidence or growth. Residual inducer, contamination, incompatible antigens and poor death confirmation can invalidate attribution. No universal DAMP cutoff establishes immunogenicity.

Necrosis describes loss of membrane integrity and tissue breakdown, rather than one molecular route. Overwhelming injury, regulated mechanisms and late secondary necrosis after apoptosis with inadequate clearance can converge on membrane loss. Necrosis is broader than necroptosis.

RIPK3-dependent MLKL activation is an example regulated necrotic mechanism. Sun and colleagues used biochemical and cellular perturbations to establish MLKL downstream of RIP3; a necrotic region or membrane-impermeant dye alone cannot establish that pathway.

Necrotic appearance can follow overwhelming injury or regulated death mechanisms. A late membrane-integrity measurement cannot reconstruct the preceding death sequence. Histology describes the sampled region; necrosis there does not establish the absence of viable tumour elsewhere, treatment success or a particular molecular pathway. Distinguish tissue appearance from a mechanism established by controlled perturbation and complementary readouts. Inflammation and antigen-specific adaptive immune protection are separate outcomes.

Histology describes the sampled region; viable tumour may remain elsewhere. A membrane-compromised fraction, qualitative tissue necrosis and method-defined necrotic area answer different questions. Handling, delayed fixation and late sampling affect interpretation, and no universal necrosis percentage identifies a death mechanism or proves treatment success. Preparing and staining a section consumes tissue, while live-cell dye assays use tested aliquots and report a defined membrane-compromised fraction. Clinical morphology and experimental pathway perturbation have different validation contexts.

HMGB1-deficient necrotic cells produced less inflammation in defined experiments. That result concerns danger signalling, rather than automatic adaptive immune memory. Dye entry after an intervention cannot establish necroptosis, vaccine activity or clinical benefit without the separate causal and host tests.

Senescent cells remain alive and metabolically active while division is durably arrested. Damage, oncogenic signals and treatment stresses can induce the state. It is distinct from death, reversible quiescence, the broader concept of dormancy and immune exhaustion, and is not a synonym for a person's age.

Low proliferation and increased p21 one day after stress do not establish durable senescence or a harmful secretory programme. Combine cell identity, longitudinal arrest or regrowth assessment and complementary features such as p16, p21, damage markers and senescence-associated beta-galactosidase. Fixed tissue cannot test later recovery, and no universal marker or arrest-duration cutoff works across contexts. Research outputs include method-defined cell fractions, marker intensities and longitudinal proliferation or regrowth. Stained sections and tested cells consume material. Secretions and their functional effects require their own readouts rather than inference from an arrest marker.

The senescence-associated secretory phenotype varies with cell, stimulus, timing and environment. In Coppé and colleagues' culture experiments, selected secretions promoted epithelial invasiveness; in Demaria and colleagues' mouse skin wounds, senescent cells and PDGF-AA supported repair. Neither experiment establishes a universal harmful mixture or a clinical instruction to remove senescent cells.

Genetically switchable blood-cancer models showed enhanced clonogenic growth after release from senescence. This supports possible escape in those systems, not inevitable restart, relapse prediction or a preferred senolytic treatment. Arrest, secretion and effects on neighbouring cells require separate tests.
